newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Chirac sees euro-zone summits overseeing EMU.
newsitem.headline: Chirac sees euro-zone summits overseeing EMU.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac said on Saturday the future members of a single European currency should hold regular summits to co-ordinate economic policy and act as a counterweight to the European central bank.

He told a news conference after an EU summit that one of the things that remained to be done in preparation for the launch of European monetary union was to establish a political authority to balance the monetary power of the independent central bank.

"In a form which has yet to be determined, the council of ministers and the council of heads of state and government of the countries which are in the euro will constitute this power opposite the central bank," he said.
He said there was general agreement on this point, although the issue, officials say, was not discussed by EU leaders at their two-day summit in Dublin.

French officials said Chirac had discussed the idea in talks with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl here and that Germany was willing to back informal arrangements to intensify co-operation among those in the euro zone.

One German diplomat had suggested ahead of the Dublin talks that Germany would back regular summits among leaders in the euro zone in return for flexibility by Paris on a budget stability pact sought by Bonn and agreed here on Friday.

One French delegation source said Chirac wanted to establish a body similar to the Group of Seven (G7) rich nations, which meets at the level either of finance ministers or heads of state and government. The G7, launched by France, has no formal secretariat, nor binding powers.
Officials say the question of how to step up co-ordination of economic policies among those inside Economic and Monetary Union looks set to become a major theme in the months ahead.
They say they are keen to ensure that other countries which do not join the single currency when it is first launched in 1999 are not left out of the decision-making process.

"We have to look and see how we can have intensified co-operation among the countries inside (the euro zone). But you cannot cut Europe in two," European Commissioner Yves Thibault de Silguy told reporters on Saturday.
In what may have been an attempt to assuage these worries, Chirac said he believed the number of countries joining the euro in 1999 would be significantly more than is currently thought.

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene suggested the question of how to co-ordinate policies inside monetary union would depend on how many countries joined in 1999. But he told reporters, "There must be a political body opposite the institutional body which is the monetary authority."
Any attempt to establish a political power to counterbalance the European Central Bank will also have to balance France and Germany's different visions of exchange rate policies.

While France wants to use the launch of the euro to push for a rise in the dollar to make European exports more competitive, Germany would never consider using exchange rates as a trade tool. Instead it gives primacy to the inflation-fighting policies of the central bank.

Chirac's aim of establishing a political grouping to co-ordinate policies inside EMU will therefore probably only be successful if it is clear it is not going to do anything to jeopardise the independence of the central bank.

France served notice on Friday that it intends to have a political input into the management of the central bank by saying a decision to name Dutchman Wim Duisenberg as head of the European Monetary Institute did not necessarily mean he would become head of the European Central Bank.
It had been assumed that Duisenberg, head of the Dutch central bank, would head the European Central Bank.
French officials said the decision about who will head the Bbank must be given serious consideration. "It is one of the most important jobs of the future," one official said.
